stats-sd-se-s1.title: How long egg white takes to set
stats-sd-se-s1.text: Heat unfolds (denatures) egg-white proteins; the unfolded chains tangle together and the clear liquid turns white and firm. A student put 5 mL of raw egg white from five different eggs into thin tubes in water baths at three temperatures and timed how long each took to turn fully opaque.

table.caption: Time for egg white to turn opaque

stats-sd-se-s2.title: Protein in two breakfast cereals
stats-sd-se-s2.text: A food lab measured the protein content of six boxes of each of two cereals, taken from different factory batches.

table.caption: Protein content (g per 100 g of cereal)

items.q: Calculate the standard deviation of the set times at 85 °C. Give your answer in seconds to one decimal place.
Calculate the standard error of the mean set time at 75 °C. Give your answer in seconds to one decimal place.
Which statement best describes the variability in these data?
options: The standard deviation is largest at 65 °C, but compared with each mean, the spread is similar at all three temperatures.
The 65 °C eggs were handled least carefully, because their standard deviation is about eight times the value measured at 85 °C.
The spread is identical at the three temperatures, because each row contains exactly five eggs.
The 85 °C data are the most variable, because their mean is the smallest of the three temperatures tested.

why.correct: In seconds, the 65 °C times spread most (s = 24.7 s). But 24.7 is about 6% of 410 s, 8.2 is about 5% of 152 s and 3.2 is about 5% of 62 s: relative to how long each takes, the eggs vary by a similar fraction.
options: Correct: compare the size of the spread with the size of the mean.
A bigger SD on a much longer time is expected; it does not by itself show sloppier handling.
The same n does not give the same spread; the SDs differ.
A small mean does not mean high variability; the 85 °C SD is the smallest.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the trend in the mean set times?
options: At higher temperatures molecules move faster, so the proteins' folds are shaken apart sooner and the unfolded chains tangle sooner.
At higher temperatures new peptide bonds form between the amino acids, linking neighboring proteins into a firm solid more quickly.
At higher temperatures the water evaporates from the tubes faster, so the egg white dries out and turns firm and white.
At higher temperatures the proteins gain extra amino acids from the water, so their primary structure changes faster.

why.correct: Heat breaks the weak interactions (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions) that hold a protein's shape. Faster molecular motion breaks them sooner, so denaturation and the visible setting happen sooner.
options: Correct: denaturation speeds up with temperature.
Denaturation breaks weak interactions; it does not make new peptide bonds, and primary structure stays the same.
The tubes sit in water baths for minutes; evaporation is not what turns egg white opaque.
Denaturation leaves the amino acid sequence unchanged.

items.q: The two cereals have nearly the same mean protein content. What do the standard deviations show?
options: Cereal B varies far more from box to box, so a single box of B is a less dependable guide to its protein content.
Cereal B contains more protein than cereal A, because a larger standard deviation means larger values overall.
Cereal A was measured less precisely, because its standard deviation is close to zero and so tells us little.
The two cereals are identical, because standard deviation does not matter when the means are the same.

why.correct: Standard deviation measures spread around the mean. B's 1.75 g/100 g is almost seven times A's 0.26 g/100 g: B's boxes range from 7.9 to 12.1.
options: Correct: same center, much wider spread.
Standard deviation is about spread, not about how large the values are.
A small SD means the boxes are consistent, which is good, not imprecise.
Equal means with very different spreads describe different products.

items.q: Calculate the standard error of the mean for cereal B. Give your answer in g/100 g to two decimal places.
The lab wants the standard error for cereal B to be about 0.36 g/100 g instead of about 0.71. Assuming the standard deviation stays near 1.75, how many boxes should it test?
options: About 24 boxes, four times as many
About 12 boxes, twice as many
About 3 boxes, half as many
About 36 boxes, six times as many

why.correct: SE = s ÷ √n. Halving SE needs √n to double, so n must be four times as large: 4 × 6 = 24. Check: 1.75 ÷ √24 = 0.357.
options: Correct: SE falls with the square root of n.
Doubling n divides SE by √2 ≈ 1.41, giving about 0.51, not 0.36.
Fewer boxes would make the standard error larger, not smaller.
Six times the boxes gives 1.75 ÷ √36 ≈ 0.29, smaller than needed.

items.q: If the lab tested 60 boxes of cereal B instead of 6, what would most likely happen to the standard deviation and the standard error?
options: The standard deviation would stay about the same, and the standard error would get much smaller.
Both the standard deviation and the standard error would get much smaller, by about the same factor.
The standard deviation would get much smaller, and the standard error would stay about the same.
Both would get larger, because more boxes give more chances for unusual values to appear.

why.correct: Standard deviation describes how much boxes really differ; testing more boxes estimates it better but does not shrink it. Standard error describes how well the mean is pinned down; it falls as 1/√n, here by about √10 ≈ 3.2.
options: Correct: SD is a property of the cereal; SE is a property of the mean.
Box-to-box variation is real; more sampling does not make boxes more alike.
This swaps the two: SE depends on n, SD does not.
Extra boxes can include unusual values, but the estimates settle down rather than grow.

items.q: In a normal distribution, about what percentage of values fall within 2 standard deviations of the mean?

why.correct: About 68% fall within ±1 SD, about 95% within ±2 SD and about 99.7% within ±3 SD.
options: Correct.
About 68% fall within ±1 SD.
50% fall on each side of the mean.
About 99.7% fall within ±3 SD.

items.q: Five 100 g samples of lentils contained 11, 13, 14, 15 and 17 g of protein. Calculate the standard deviation in grams, to two decimal places.

why.correct: Mean = 70 ÷ 5 = 14 g. Squared deviations: 9, 1, 0, 1, 9; sum = 20. Divide by n − 1 = 4: 5. s = √5 = 2.236, which rounds to 2.24 g.

items.q: A student calculating a standard deviation from 5 values divides the sum of squared deviations by 5 instead of 4. How does her answer compare with the correct value?
options: It is a little too small, because dividing by n instead of n − 1 gives a smaller result.
It is a little too large, because dividing by a larger number makes the answer larger.
It is the same, because n and n − 1 differ by just 1, which has no effect on the square root.
It is too small by a factor of 5, because each squared deviation was divided by an extra 5.

why.correct: Dividing the same sum by 5 instead of 4 gives 80% of the variance, so the square root is √0.8 ≈ 0.89 of the correct SD: about 11% too small.
options: Correct.
Dividing by a larger number gives a smaller answer.
With small samples the difference matters: √(4/5) ≈ 0.89.
Only the divisor changed from 4 to 5, so the variance shrinks to 4/5 of its value, not 1/5.

items.q: Two sets of five measurements have the same mean of 50 g. Set X: 49, 50, 50, 50, 51. Set Y: 40, 45, 50, 55, 60. Without calculating, which is true?
options: Set Y has the larger standard deviation, because its values sit farther from the mean.
The two sets have the same standard deviation, because they have the same mean.
Set X has the larger standard deviation, because more of its values equal the mean.
Neither set has a standard deviation, because five values are too few to calculate one.

why.correct: Standard deviation grows with the typical distance from the mean. Y's values are up to 10 g away; X's at most 1 g.
options: Correct.
Same mean does not mean same spread.
Values equal to the mean add zero to the sum of squares, which lowers the SD.
Any sample of two or more values has a standard deviation.

items.q: A student says: "The standard error is smaller than the standard deviation, so it is a better measure of how variable my eggs were." What is the best response?
options: SD describes how much individual eggs varied; SE describes how precisely the mean is known, so they answer different questions.
The student is right, because a smaller number shows that the measurements were more precise, so it is the better one to report for eggs.
Standard error is larger than standard deviation for small samples, so the student has made a calculation mistake.
The two are the same quantity written two ways, so it makes no difference which one is used.

why.correct: SE = s ÷ √n is always smaller than s for n > 1, but it does not describe the eggs. It describes uncertainty in the mean. To describe variability among eggs, report the SD.
options: Correct: SD for spread of individuals, SE for precision of the mean.
SE is smaller because of the division by √n, not because the eggs varied less.
For n > 1, √n > 1, so SE is smaller than SD.
They differ by a factor of √n and mean different things.

items.q: Put the steps for calculating the standard error of the mean in order.
options: Calculate the mean, x̄.
Subtract the mean from each value and square each result.
Add the squares and divide by n − 1.
Take the square root to get s.
Divide s by √n.

why.correct: Mean, squared deviations, sum ÷ (n − 1), square root (s), then SE = s ÷ √n.

items.q: The student adds a sixth egg at 85 °C that sets in 61 s. What happens to the mean and the standard deviation?
options: The mean drops slightly and the standard deviation drops slightly, because 61 s is close to the mean.
The mean stays at 62 s and the standard deviation rises, because adding any value adds spread.
The mean drops by 1 s and the standard deviation stays at 3.2 s, because the mean depends on n and the SD does not.
Both stay the same, because a single value has too small an effect to change either statistic.

why.correct: New mean = 371 ÷ 6 = 61.8 s. The new value sits about 1 s from the mean, closer than most values, and n − 1 grows from 4 to 5, so s falls from about 3.16 to about 2.86 s.
options: Correct: a value near the mean lowers the SD.
The mean moves from 62 to 61.8 s, and a value close to the mean lowers the SD rather than raising it.
The new mean is 61.8 s, not 61 s, and the SD changes because n − 1 and the sum of squares both change.
Both statistics change a little; they use every value.
